papers.title: IMPROVING SENIOR HIGH SCHOOL STUDENTS’ CRITICAL THINKING SKILLS AND LEARNING ENGAGEMENT IN STOICHIOMETRY THROUGH PROBLEM-BASED LEARNING: A CLASSROOM ACTION RESEARCH
papers.abstract: Previous studies have shown that Problem-Based Learning (PBL) effectively improves students’ critical thinking skills, learning outcomes, and engagement in stoichiometry. However, previous studies have mainly focused on learning outcomes. At the same time, the implementation of PBL through Classroom Action Research (CAR), which emphasizes continuous reflection and instructional improvement across cycles, has received limited attention. This study aimed to improve Grade 10 students’ critical thinking skills and learning activities in stoichiometry by implementing the PBL model. This study employed the Classroom Action Research (CAR) method involving 20 Grade 10 students and was conducted in two cycles, each consisting of planning, implementation, observation, and reflection. The success criteria were determined based on improvements in students’ critical thinking skills, learning activities, and learning mastery from Cycle I to Cycle II. Data were collected using pretests, posttests, student worksheets (LKPD), and observation sheets. The average posttest score increased from 82.50 in Cycle I to 85.25 in Cycle II, while student learning activities improved from 46.00% to 68.06%. The N-gain values were 0.254 in Cycle I and 0.175 in Cycle II, both categorized as low, indicating limited improvement due to students’ relatively high initial achievement. In addition, learning mastery increased from 80% to 85%. These findings indicate that implementing the PBL model through continuous reflection and instructional improvement can enhance students’ critical thinking skills and learning activities. papers.title: Engineering acoustic attenuation in TPMS structures for flow-permeable noise barriers
papers.abstract: Effective noise control without compromising airflow is increasingly required in the built environment, particularly for HVAC systems, facades, and flow-permeable noise barriers. Conventional sandwich structures with face sheets and cores provide high sound insulation but obstruct airflow, limiting their use in these applications. This study investigates the sound transmission loss (STL) of core-only triply periodic minimal surface (TPMS) acoustic metamaterials, including Primitive (P), Neovius (N), hybrid P+N, Diamond (D), F Rhombic Dodecahedron (FRD), and Fischer Koch Schoen (FKS) topologies. STL was evaluated numerically using pressure acoustics and thermoviscous models and validated experimentally using impedance tube measurements, while airflow performance was assessed through permeability and transport properties. Numerical predictions showed good agreement with experiments for all six investigated topologies at H = 20 mm. In the numerical topology comparison at H = 15 mm, topology N achieved the highest acoustic attenuation but the lowest permeability. For the baseline Neovius configuration ( L = 5 mm, φ = 80%, H = 15 mm), the strongest STL response occurs approximately within the 3–4 kHz range of the investigated 1–6 kHz band. Increasing thickness and decreasing porosity shift the attenuation toward lower frequencies, whereas increasing cell size reduces thermoviscous dissipation and overall STL. Further extension toward lower frequencies may be possible through appropriate tuning of TPMS topology and geometric parameters. The present results, therefore, establish a design framework for tuning flow-permeable TPMS structures to targeted acoustic frequency ranges while maintaining interconnected airflow.

papers.title: Experiment, simulation, analytical prediction and a PINN surrogate for generated wave analysis in a numerical wave tank with box-shaped plunger wavemaker type
papers.abstract: This study develops and validates a two-dimensional numerical wave tank (NWT) as a practical calibration framework for regular waves generated by a box-shaped vertical plunger wavemaker. Regular waves are generated by a box-shaped plunger wavemaker driven by a prescribed sinusoidal motion (period T ), and the resulting wave characteristics are quantified in terms of wave amplitude, wavelength, and waveform evolution. A mesh-sensitivity study is first performed to ensure solution reliability, after which the validated numerical model is shown to reproduce the experimentally observed wave period and free-surface response with good agreement. Building on the principle of mass conservation, an analytical expression is derived to establish an explicit relationship between the plunger stroke amplitude S and the generated wave height H , with the wavenumber obtained from the linear dispersion relation. Parametric results confirm an approximately linear dependence between H and S under fixed T , while increasing discrepancies are observed at larger strokes as the operating conditions approach the limit of linear wave theory, as assessed via the Le Méhauté diagram. To reduce reliance on computationally intensive simulations during parameter exploration, a parametric physics-informed neural network (PINN) surrogate is further introduced to predict the harmonic wave response while enforcing the governing physics and boundary conditions, and is anchored by the derived H − S scaling within the linear regime. The proposed analytical predictor and the PINN-enabled surrogate together provide a rapid, practical workflow for screening wavemaker settings.

summary_zh.result: 解析式与PINN代理均能快速预测规则波响应，线性区吻合良好。
summary_zh.validation: 通过网格敏感性分析、实验对比及解析解交叉验证。

summary_en.motivation: To reduce the computational cost of exploring wavemaker settings in numerical wave tanks.
summary_en.method: A 2D numerical wave tank is validated, an analytical stroke-to-wave-height relation is derived from mass conservation, and a parametric PINN surrogate is trained to predict harmonic wave response.
summary_en.result: The analytical predictor and PINN surrogate reproduce wave characteristics rapidly, with good agreement in the linear regime and growing deviations at large strokes.
summary_en.validation: Validated via mesh-sensitivity study, experimental free-surface comparison, and cross-checking against the derived analytical scaling.
